findings.title: Every authenticated request builds one or more brand-new Supabase clients, each parsing the CA bundle into a fresh SSLContext on the event loop; GET /history does it 3x
findings.evidence: auth_service.py:26-30 `def get_auth_client() -> Client: ... return create_client(SUPABASE_URL, SUPABASE_ANON_KEY)` — no cache. verify_token() calls it at auth_service.py:256 (`client = get_auth_client()`), and verify_token runs via get_current_user (auth_routes.py:275) on EVERY authed request. database_service.py:48-53 get_user_supabase_client does the same (`client = create_client(...)`, 16 call sites) while only get_admin_supabase_client (db_service.py:38-45) caches a singleton. cProfile of 3x create_client: 1.202s of 1.341s total in `httpx/_config.py:102(load_ssl_context_verify)`. Isolated `ssl.create_default_context(certifi.where())` = 537 ms median; exactly 1 SSLContext per create_client.
findings.repro: python scratchpad/m22-review/ls-db/meas_client.py and meas_ssl.py (written this session). Measured: create_client() 10x warm = median 507 ms with ZERO network; fresh-client-per-query 532 ms vs reused-client 140 ms (delta 392 ms); simulating GET /history's 3 constructions = 1,822 ms median. Windows dev box, LOCAL OFF-LOCK env (supabase 2.28.0 vs lock 2.31.0, httpx 0.27.0 vs 0.28.1).
findings.impact: Structural, not incidental: on the single-worker uvicorn every authed request pays N synchronous SSLContext builds plus N cold TLS handshakes (each new httpx.Client has its own connection pool — verified `s1._transport is not s2._transport`). GET /history pays 3 (verify_token + get_user_comparisons + get_user_comparison_count); /home/savings, /home/smart-pick, /profile/* pay 2. Critically this is NOT covered by run_db: at auth_service.py:256 the construction runs inline and only the `client.auth.get_user(...)` call is wrapped, so flipping ENABLE_SYNC_DB_OFFLOAD does NOT move it off the loop. This is a hard multiplier on the ~10 compares/min deployment-wide ceiling M18 modelled, and it is the one part of that ceiling nobody has costed. Magnitude on Railway/Linux will be well below 500 ms (CA parsing is much cheaper there) but the per-request count and the on-loop placement are the same.
findings.fix: Cache both auth clients the way get_admin_supabase_client already does: memoise get_auth_client() and get_admin_client() in auth_service as module singletons (they are stateless w.r.t. the request — only the anon/service key is baked in). For get_user_supabase_client, keep the per-request JWT binding but stop rebuilding the transport: construct ONE module-level httpx client / SSLContext and pass it into create_client via ClientOptions(httpx_client=...), or cache a single anon Client and call .postgrest.auth(token) per request only if the supabase-py version guarantees no cross-request token leakage — verify that before shipping, since a shared client with per-request auth() is a tenant-bleed risk under concurrency. Ship behind ENABLE_POOLED_SUPABASE_CLIENTS (default OFF) and land it BEFORE the #114 limiter re-key, per the M18 ordering rule that offloads must be active first. This is the concrete mechanism behind open issue #73 (pooled httpx).
findings.test_first: A test that monkeypatches ssl.SSLContext.__new__ (or supabase.create_client) with a counter, drives GET /api/v1/history through the real FastAPI TestClient with a valid token, and asserts the counter increments by 0 across two successive requests once the flag is ON (and by 3 today with it OFF) — pins both the current behaviour and the fix.
findings.dedupe: new — adjacent to open #73 (pooled httpx + bound GCC endpoint) and #71 (Redis/Supabase off loop), but both of those are about the CALL; this is about the CLIENT CONSTRUCTION, which run_db explicitly does not cover. Not in the M18 175-row set or M13.

findings.title: /home/savings caches its DEGRADED zero payload for 6 hours, so one Supabase hiccup hides a user's savings banner until the next day
findings.evidence: home_routes.py:227-241 flag-ON branch: `except Exception as exc: logger.error("[home/savings] aggregate RPC failed..."); total_savings, decisions_count = 0.0, 0` (line 231) then UNCONDITIONALLY `payload = {...}` and `await _redis_set_async(cache_key, json.dumps(payload), ex=_SAVINGS_TTL_SECONDS)` (line 238). Legacy branch identical: line 261 `rows = []` on failure, then line 285 caches the resulting zeros. `_SAVINGS_TTL_SECONDS = 6 * 60 * 60` (home_routes.py:120) with the comment 'Lengthened 5min -> 6h'.
findings.repro: Static read of the two branches at HEAD plus a live RPC probe: `c.rpc('home_savings_aggregate', {'p_user_id': ...})` returns PGRST202 'Could not find the function public.home_savings_aggregate(p_user_id) in the schema cache' — migration 036 is not applied, so the flag-ON path fails 100% of the time today and every failure would be cached as zeros.
findings.impact: Two live consequences. (a) TODAY on the legacy path: any transient Supabase error on the one uncached savings request pins savings_bhd=0, decisions_count=0, threshold_met=false into Redis for 6 hours — the SavingsBanner disappears entirely (the frontend hides it below threshold), and because bust-on-write only fires on save/delete, a user who runs no comparison sees nothing for the full 6h. #116 lengthened this TTL from 5 min to 6 h, so the blast radius of an already-existing bug was amplified 72x in the same change that was meant to make the endpoint cheaper. (b) WHEN the flag is flipped: because 036 is unapplied, EVERY user's first /home/savings call caches zeros for 6h, and applying 036 afterwards does not clear them — the product looks like it lost everyone's savings history for most of a day.
findings.fix: Never cache a degraded result. In both branches, set a `degraded = True` marker in the except handler and skip the `_redis_set_async` call entirely when it is set (serve the zeros for this one request only), or cache with a short punitive TTL (30-60 s) so a transient error self-heals. Separately, make the flag-ON path fall back to the legacy scan rather than to zeros when the RPC raises PGRST202/PGRST404 specifically — a missing function is a deploy-ordering error, not a data answer. Gate the fallback under the existing ENABLE_HOME_SAVINGS_AGGREGATE so flag-OFF stays byte-identical, and add a startup assertion (or a /health sub-check) that the RPC exists before the flag is allowed to be ON.
findings.test_first: Patch home_routes.run_db to raise, call home_savings via TestClient, and assert (i) the response is the zero payload AND (ii) home_routes._redis_set_async was never awaited — red today on both branches. Second test: patch the RPC to raise APIError(PGRST202) with the flag ON and assert the legacy scan ran and returned the real total.
findings.dedupe: new — #116 is closed and covered the cost of the scan and the bust-on-write contract; neither #116 nor the M18 set noticed that the degraded path writes the cache, nor that the 5min->6h change multiplied it.

findings.title: PostgREST silently truncates at 1000 rows: the LIVE /home/savings scan stops counting a user's savings at 1000 comparisons and reports a wrong total with no error
findings.evidence: home_routes.py:246-256 (the flag-OFF path that RUNS in prod — ENABLE_HOME_SAVINGS_AGGREGATE is absent from the Railway web var list): `client.table("comparisons").select("full_response").eq("user_id", user_id).eq("schema_version", 2).execute()` — no .limit(), no .range(). The code comment even says 'Unbounded in rows and payload' but treats that as a cost problem only. MEASURED cap: unbounded search_logs select returned 1000 of 16,283 rows; explicit .limit(2000) -> 1000; .limit(5000) -> 1000; .limit(999) -> 999.
findings.repro: python scratchpad/m22-review/ls-db/meas2.py and meas_cap.py. Cap demonstrated on this exact Supabase project. Cost model using the measured median full_response of 19,026 B: 27 rows (whole prod today) = heaviest single user 205,685 B measured; 1,000 comparisons for one user = ~19.0 MB transferred and the answer is still exactly right at the cap boundary; 10,000 = still 1,000 rows / ~19.0 MB, savings under-reported by ~90%; 100,000 = still 1,000 rows / ~19.0 MB, under-reported by ~99%.
findings.impact: The failure mode is not the cost (which plateaus at ~19 MB per uncached call), it is CORRECTNESS: past 1,000 saved comparisons a user's savings_bhd and decisions_count silently freeze and then drift ever further below the truth, with a 200 response and no log line. It arrives exactly when the product succeeds. Today the ceiling is 10 rows for the heaviest of 6 users so nothing is wrong yet — this is latent, which is why it is P2 and not P1. The same silent cap applies to the other 20 unbounded table reads enumerated in classify.txt; the two that would be wrong FIRST are this one and /profile/monthly-stats (LS-DB-QUERIES-08).
findings.fix: Apply migration 036 and turn ENABLE_HOME_SAVINGS_AGGREGATE ON — that is the real fix and it already exists; the aggregate is computed in Postgres and returns one row, so no cap applies. Until then, the legacy branch must not pretend to be complete: add `.limit(1000)` explicitly and, when exactly 1000 rows come back, either page with .range() until exhausted or stamp `"truncated": true` into the payload so the banner can say 'your last 1,000 decisions'. Do NOT leave the implicit cap in place. Also add a repo-wide lint/test that fails on any `.select(...)` reaching `.execute()` with no `.limit`/`.range`/`.single`/`.maybe_single` on the 21 sites listed in classify.txt.
findings.test_first: Seed 1,001 v2 comparison rows for one user in a test Supabase (or stub the client to return exactly 1000 rows for an unbounded select), call /home/savings, and assert decisions_count == 1001 — red today, and red in a way that no existing test catches because every fixture is far under the cap.
findings.dedupe: new — #116 (closed) named this query as unbounded in rows and payload and built the aggregate to fix the COST; the silent-truncation CORRECTNESS consequence of the 1000-row cap is not stated in #116, the M18 set, or M13.

findings.title: Behaviour-profile recompute aborts on its FIRST query against three columns that do not exist, costing ~165 ms per compare and leaving personalization dead for 100% of users
findings.evidence: scs.py:4545-4547 selects `category_used, products, created_at` from comparisons, `useful` from comparison_feedback, and `event_type, metadata` from user_events. LIVE probe: comparisons has exactly 9 columns and `category_used` -> 42703 'column comparisons.category_used does not exist'; `products` -> 42703; user_events' real column is `event_data`, `metadata` -> 42703. Only the comparison_feedback select is valid. Because the three run_db calls are SEQUENTIAL and the whole block sits in one `try`, the 42703 on line 4545 raises straight to `except Exception as e: logger.warning(f"Failed to update behavior profile: {e}")` at line 4553 — lines 4546-4552 never execute, so `users.update({'behavior_profile': profile})` NEVER RUNS.
findings.repro: python scratchpad/m22-review/ls-db/meas_probe.py + meas_cost.py against prod Supabase (SELECT only). The failing query's round trip: [1620, 166, 165, 137, 137] ms, median 165. And the decisive number: `users` total = 18, `behavior_profile` NON-NULL = 0.
findings.impact: Answers the lane's question precisely. COST PER COMPARE = exactly ONE wasted Supabase round trip (~165 ms measured dev-box, MODELLED lower from Railway), not four — the abort is early, so the phantom columns are cheaper than they look. The real damage is the silence: 0 of 18 users have ever had a behavior_profile written, so scs._fetch_behavior_profile (line 4524, which reads a column that DOES exist) always returns None, the /home/smart-pick dimension_sensitivity Tier-2 fallback (home_routes.py:628-640) never fires, and every 'personalized' code path downstream runs on defaults. Personalization is not degraded, it has never once worked in production. Two of the three phantom columns are the same class of bug as the `response_data` phantom that broke referral landings (fixed 2026-09-02) — the pattern is unfixed.
findings.fix: Map the three selects onto the real schema: `comparisons` has no category or products column, so category/product signal must come out of `full_response` (jsonb) — either select `full_response` and extract in behavior_service, or add a generated/derived column in a new migration; `user_events.metadata` is simply the wrong name for `event_data` and is a one-word fix. Do NOT ship the rename alone — with only the user_events fix the chain still dies on line 4545. Also split the single try into per-query try/except so one bad select degrades to an empty list instead of silently cancelling the profile write, and raise the log from warning to Sentry (open #68) since a 100%-failing write produced no alert for months. Fix under the existing #65 issue and re-verify by asserting behavior_profile is non-null for a test user after one compare.
findings.test_first: An integration test (live_db marker) that runs _update_behavior_profile for a seeded user against the real schema and asserts `users.behavior_profile` is non-null afterwards. A cheaper unit guard that would ALSO have caught this: a schema-contract test that reads the column list of each table from information_schema and asserts every column name appearing in a `.select(...)` string literal across app/ exists — that single test pins all three phantoms and the `response_data` class of bug for good.
findings.dedupe: known:#65 (behavior profile reads phantom columns, personalization DEAD) — STILL-OPEN. Fresh evidence this session: the exact three phantom columns named and confirmed live against prod schema, the abort-on-first-query semantics (so the cost is 1 round trip not 4), the measured 165 ms, and the decisive 0-of-18 behavior_profile population. Also touches #74 (bound behaviour-profile recompute), which is moot while the recompute never completes.

findings.title: GET /history selects * (pulling ~19 KB of full_response per row) to build a summary that never reads it, then spends a second client and an exact COUNT on the same page
findings.evidence: database_service.py:248-260 `client.table("comparisons").select("*")...range(offset, offset+limit-1)`. The consumer, history_routes.py:106-125, builds each summary from only id, query, product_names, input_type, created_at plus winner_index and two image URLs derived from full_response.products — it never returns full_response. history_routes.py:128 then calls `get_user_comparison_count(...)` which at database_service.py:448-455 constructs ANOTHER get_user_supabase_client and runs `.select("id", count="exact")`. limit is Query(20, ge=1, le=50).
findings.repro: Measured whole-row select('*') size over all 27 recorded rows: median 19,359 B, mean 18,307 B, max 25,322 B (meas2.py). At the max page size of 50 that is ~968 KB pulled from Supabase to emit roughly 8 KB of JSON — a ~120x over-fetch. At the default 20 it is ~387 KB.
findings.impact: Three costs on the single-worker loop for one screen open: ~387-968 KB of wire transfer and jsonb deserialisation that is thrown away; a second create_client (see LS-DB-QUERIES-01, ~2 SSLContexts for this one route on top of verify_token's); and a `count="exact"` which makes Postgres do a real COUNT over the user's filtered set on every page rather than once. The index (user_id, schema_version, created_at DESC) from migration 020 covers the WHERE+ORDER correctly, so this is pure payload and round-trip waste, not a plan problem. It scales with history length in bytes-per-page and is the single largest avoidable transfer on any user-facing read.
findings.fix: Project only what the route uses. The two image URLs and winner_index come out of full_response.products, so either (a) select `id, query, product_names, input_type, created_at, full_response->'winner_index', full_response->'products'` using PostgREST's jsonb path projection to avoid hauling verdicts/specs/reviews, or (b) better, persist winner_index and the two image URLs as real columns at save time (a small migration) and drop full_response from the list query entirely. Reuse ONE client for both the page and the count by threading it through get_user_comparisons/get_user_comparison_count instead of each calling the factory. And return the count only when offset==0, or switch to `count='planned'`, so paging does not re-COUNT.
findings.test_first: A test that stubs the supabase client and asserts the select string passed for GET /history does NOT contain '*' and DOES contain exactly the projected columns; plus a call-counter assertion that get_user_supabase_client is invoked once, not twice, per /history request.
findings.dedupe: new — M13/M18 covered the history route's rendering and pagination but not its projection or its double client construction.

findings.title: product_prices is append-only with no retention and the hot read sorts up to 416 rows to return 1, because the only index lacks fetched_at
findings.evidence: product_data_service.py:128-137 reads `client.table("product_prices").select(cols).eq("product_key", pk).eq("region", region).order("fetched_at", desc=True).limit(1)`. The write at product_data_service.py:208 is a plain `.insert(row)` — never an upsert, so every price fetch appends a new row forever. The only matching index is `CREATE INDEX idx_prices_key_region ON product_prices (product_key, region)` (migration 012); `idx_prices_fetched ON product_prices (fetched_at DESC)` is a separate single-column index. Neither is the composite the query needs.
findings.repro: Full 3,945-row scan via range() paging (meas_cap.py): 735 distinct (product_key, region) pairs; rows per pair max=416, median=2; top ten [416,198,187,96,94,73,47,40,32,31]. 81.4% of rows can never be returned by a .limit(1) newest-first read.
findings.impact: For the hottest key Postgres must fetch all 416 index entries for that (product_key, region), heap-access them for fetched_at, sort, and discard 415 — twice per compare (once per product), on the L2 lookup that is supposed to be the CHEAP path that avoids a scrape. The table has no cleanup job of any kind (grepped all migrations and app/ for delete/retention/cleanup/purge/prune — only delete_user_cascade exists), so both the row count and the per-key sort depth grow without bound; the newest row is dated 2026-09-01, i.e. it is still growing. At 3,945 rows this is microseconds, but the growth is unbounded and the read is on the critical path of every comparison.
findings.fix: Two changes, both small. (1) Add `CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS idx_prices_key_region_fetched ON product_prices (product_key, region, fetched_at DESC);` in a new migration — this makes the hot read a single index-only fetch of the first entry regardless of history depth, and makes idx_prices_key_region redundant (drop it in the same migration). (2) Add retention: either a scheduled job that keeps the newest N (say 10) rows per (product_key, region) and deletes the rest, or — since the read only ever wants the newest — change the write to an upsert on (product_key, region) and keep history in a separate append table only if the price-history feature is actually wanted. Prefer the index first (zero behaviour change, ship immediately); gate any deletion behind an explicit flag and a dry-run count.
findings.test_first: There is no cheap unit test for a missing index. The honest red test is a live_db benchmark: seed 500 rows for one (product_key, region), time get_cached_price, then assert it stays under a fixed budget — it fails before the index and passes after. Pair it with a static test asserting the migration set contains an index whose columns are exactly (product_key, region, fetched_at) so the index cannot be dropped silently.
findings.dedupe: new — #57 (L2 promote freshness) and #56 (category into _get_price) touch this module's semantics, not its index or its growth. Not in M18/M13.

findings.title: user_events has no index of any kind, yet is read with eq(user_id) + order(created_at DESC) on the compare path and written once per comparison
findings.evidence: Grepped every migration for `user_events`: it appears only in 010_enable_rls.sql (RLS enable + two policies), 013 (a view join), and 025 (cascade delete). There is NO CREATE INDEX on user_events anywhere in the 31 migration files, while comparisons, search_logs, referral_invites, admin_audit_log, re_engagement_events, user_preference_history and verdict_critiques all get (user_id, created_at DESC)-shaped indexes. The queries: scs.py:4547 `.eq("user_id", user_id).order("created_at", desc=True).limit(200)` and admin_routes.py:375 `.eq("user_id", uid).limit(50)`. The write is feedback_service.py:194 `.insert(record)`, fired once per saved comparison via save_comparison_and_track_cohort, plus a batch insert at feedback_service.py:227.
findings.repro: Static: full grep of migrations/ for user_events shown above. Live: table currently holds 146 rows; the eq(user_id)+order(created_at)+limit(200) query measures 136-153 ms, indistinguishable from any other round trip at this size (meas_cost.py) — which is exactly why the missing index is invisible today.
findings.impact: Every read is a sequential scan plus a sort. At 146 rows that is free, so nothing is broken now. But user_events is written once per comparison (comparison_completed) plus once per analytics batch, so it grows strictly faster than the comparisons table; migration 013's vw_cohort_feedback_lift view joins it, and admin_routes.py:362-380 loops over up to N users issuing one user_events query EACH inside a Python for-loop (an N+1 that becomes N sequential seq-scans). This is the cheapest fix in the lane and the one most likely to be forgotten until it is a production incident, because there is no failing signal until the table is large.
findings.fix: Add a migration with `CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS idx_user_events_user_created ON user_events (user_id, created_at DESC);` — this covers scs.py:4547, admin_routes.py:375 and the cohort view join. Add `CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS idx_user_events_comparison ON user_events (comparison_id);` too, since 013's view and the cascade delete both key on it. No code change and no flag needed — an index addition is behaviour-preserving. Do it in the same migration that fixes the phantom `metadata` column in LS-DB-QUERIES-04, since neither is useful without the other.
findings.test_first: A static test over migrations/ asserting that every table read with a `.eq(<col>).order(<col2>)` pattern in app/ has a migration index whose leading columns match — generated from the enumeration in this review, it would flag user_events today and prevent the next table from shipping without one.
findings.dedupe: new — no prior review enumerated indexes per table. Adjacent to #74 (bound behaviour-profile recompute) only in that both touch this query.

findings.title: /profile/monthly-stats runs an unbounded full_response month scan with zero run_db coverage — profile_routes is the only route module that never offloads a single query
findings.evidence: profile_routes.py:314-322 `client.table("comparisons").select("full_response, created_at").eq("user_id", user_id).eq("schema_version", 2).gte("created_at", month_start).execute()` — assigned directly, not `await run_db(...)`. Same at profile_routes.py:190 (recent-decisions), :340 (referral_redemptions, also unbounded) and :483. profile_routes.py does not appear in the list of 9 modules that import run_db (home_routes, audit_service, auth_service, database_service, feedback_service, product_data_service, referral_service, structured_comparison_service, usage_service) — grepped `from app.utils.db_offload import run_db` across app/. It also calls the sync `_redis_get(cache_key)` at :299 where home_routes uses `_redis_get_async`.
findings.repro: Static read of profile_routes.py at HEAD plus the run_db importer grep. Cost model with the measured median full_response of 19,026 B: /profile/recent-decisions pulls 3 blobs = ~57 KB constant; /profile/monthly-stats pulls every v2 comparison in the current month with no limit — bounded today only by how much a user compares in 30 days, and subject to the same silently-capped 1000 rows (~19 MB) as LS-DB-QUERIES-03.
findings.impact: Two distinct problems in one module. (a) The month scan is the second unbounded user-facing full_response scan; it hauls whole verdict payloads to sum two floats per row, and it will silently under-report savings for any user exceeding 1000 comparisons in a month. (b) More consequential for the load story: ENABLE_SYNC_DB_OFFLOAD is the deployment's lever for getting blocking DB work off the single event loop, and flipping it moves NOTHING in profile_routes — 4 blocking Supabase calls and a blocking Redis GET stay on the loop, plus the client construction from LS-DB-QUERIES-01. Anyone measuring the flag's effect will conclude it under-delivers without knowing which sites were never wired.
findings.fix: Wire profile_routes into the existing offload: import run_db and _redis_get_async/_redis_set_async (or the module-local dispatch idiom home_routes already uses, so tests can patch a module-level symbol in both branches) and wrap all four .execute() calls plus the cache reads — flag OFF stays byte-identical by construction, so this is a safe no-flag change. Separately, replace the monthly-stats scan with a month-scoped variant of the migration-036 aggregate (add a p_month_start argument, or a second function) so the endpoint stops moving verdict blobs to compute a sum; keep it dark under the same ENABLE_HOME_SAVINGS_AGGREGATE-style flag until 036 is actually applied.
findings.test_first: A test that patches app.utils.db_offload.sync_db_offload_enabled to True, monkeypatches asyncio.to_thread with a counter, hits GET /api/v1/profile/monthly-stats and asserts the counter is >0 — red today (zero offloads), green once wired. Plus the 1000-row truncation test from LS-DB-QUERIES-03 applied to the month window.
findings.dedupe: new — M18's LS-event-loop findings and #71 established the blocking-on-loop theme and #115/M13-05 built run_db; no prior review enumerated WHICH call sites were left unwired, and profile_routes was not touched in 593ec1e..76ace90 so it was never re-checked.

findings.title: Admin 'top queries' ranks an arbitrary unordered 1000-row slice of 16,283 search_logs and reports it as popular queries
findings.evidence: analytics_service.py:59-77 get_popular_queries: `client.table("search_logs").select("query, input_type").execute()` with no .limit(), no .gte(), and no .order() — then `Counter(...).most_common(limit)` over whatever came back. Three sibling functions have the same shape with only a date filter: :18 (success/cost/duration over `since`), :86 (cost trends), :125 (error stats). analytics_service.py:163 scans the whole `products` table unbounded.
findings.repro: Live SELECT replication of the exact query shapes (meas2.py, meas_cost.py): the unbounded `select('query, input_type')` returned 1000 rows of 16,283 — 6.1% of the table. The 30-day window at :18 returned 717 rows (under the cap, currently honest) but the same query with since=2026-06-01 returned 1000 of 13,237 actual. So the truncation is not hypothetical: it is already active on the popular-queries call today and becomes active on the trend calls as soon as the window is widened past ~1000 rows.
findings.impact: The admin analytics surface is quietly wrong, and wrong in a way that looks plausible. Because there is no ORDER BY, the 1000 rows PostgREST returns are whatever the plan yields — typically the physical/insert order, i.e. the OLDEST 1000 of 16,283 — so 'popular queries' reflects mid-June traffic and nothing since. get_cost_trends and get_error_stats (exposed at admin_routes.py:72 and :83) silently drop everything past 1000 rows in any window that large, under-reporting spend and error volume with no indicator. Anyone using this dashboard to decide whether the product is working is reading a stale 6% sample. Admin-only, so not user-facing — hence P2, not P1.
findings.fix: Stop pulling rows to count them. Each of these four is an aggregate: push them into Postgres as SECURITY DEFINER RPCs the way migration 036 does for savings (a GROUP BY query for popular queries; SUM/COUNT grouped by day for cost trends; COUNT grouped by error_message for error stats) and return a handful of rows. If an RPC is too much for now, the minimum honest fix is to add an explicit `.order('created_at', desc=True).limit(1000)` so the sample is at least the MOST RECENT 1000 and to stamp `"truncated": true, "sampled_rows": 1000` into every response so the dashboard cannot present a sample as a total. Same treatment for the unbounded `products` scan at :163.
findings.test_first: Stub the client to return exactly 1000 rows for an unbounded select and assert get_popular_queries either raises, pages, or sets truncated=true — red today, since it silently returns a top-20 computed from the partial set.
findings.dedupe: new — open #66 (admin cost meters wrong) covers the cost METERS' arithmetic; the silent 1000-row truncation feeding four analytics functions is a different mechanism and is not in #66, M18 or M13.

findings.title: Admin cost dashboard asks for 2000 comparisons and PostgREST hands back exactly 1000, so the monthly spend figure is silently halved at scale
findings.evidence: admin_routes.py:729-737 `client.table("comparisons").select("created_at, full_response").gte("created_at", cutoff_iso).limit(2000).execute()` feeding a Python loop that sums `full_response.metadata.total_cost` into openai_total and daily_burn. The author explicitly chose 2000 as the bound.
findings.repro: MEASURED that an explicit limit above the server cap is silently reduced: `.limit(2000)` -> 1000 rows, `.limit(5000)` -> 1000 rows, `.limit(999)` -> 999 rows (meas_cap.py, against this Supabase project). So the requested bound is not the effective bound and nothing says so.
findings.impact: An explicit .limit() reads like a deliberate safety bound and is treated as one by every reader of this code, but half of it is fiction. Once the window contains more than 1000 comparisons the dashboard's openai_total and daily_burn are computed from an unordered ~1000-row subset and under-report spend without any indicator — on a cost dashboard, silently under-reporting is the worst possible direction to be wrong in. Secondary cost: at the measured median full_response of 19,026 B this route pulls ~19 MB (1000 rows) to sum one float per row, on the shared event loop, and it is not run_db-wrapped. Admin-only, days is capped at 90, and prod traffic is currently near zero, so this is P2.
findings.fix: Same shape as LS-DB-QUERIES-09: this is an aggregate, so move it into Postgres — a SECURITY DEFINER RPC that returns (day, sum_cost, sample_count) grouped by day over the cutoff, which is one small round trip and no cap. As an interim, page with `.range()` until a short page is returned and add `.order('created_at', desc=True)` so a truncated result is at least the most recent window, and surface `truncated`/`rows_scanned` in the response body. Also project `full_response->'metadata'->>'total_cost'` instead of the whole blob so the transfer drops from ~19 MB to a few hundred KB, and route it through run_db.
findings.test_first: A test asserting that when the stubbed client returns exactly the requested limit the route either pages again or marks the result truncated — and, more valuable, a shared regression test that no `.limit(n)` with n > 1000 exists anywhere in app/, since the value is unachievable and therefore always misleading.
findings.dedupe: new — related to open #66 (admin cost meters wrong) but a distinct mechanism (transport-level truncation of a deliberate bound, not meter arithmetic).

findings.title: P3 sweep — five smaller DB-layer defects: no retention on any growth table, smart-pick over-fetch, an exception per L2 specs miss, an admin N+1, and an unbounded fingerprint fan-in
findings.evidence: (a) RETENTION: grepped all 31 migrations and app/ for delete/retention/cleanup/purge/prune/vacuum — the only deletion path is delete_user_cascade (GDPR, per-user). search_logs 16,283 / product_prices 3,945 / admin_audit_log 1,439 / user_events 146 all grow monotonically with no job, no TTL and no partitioning; #80 (cron failure visibility) exists but there is no cron to fail. (b) SMART-PICK: home_routes.py:653 `.select("id, full_response, created_at")...limit(5)` pulls 5 whole verdict blobs = ~95 KB measured (5 x 19,026 B) to choose one card, and neither it nor the users read at home_routes.py:612 is run_db-wrapped even though the savings query in the same file is. (c) L2 MISS COST: product_data_service.py:76 uses `.single()` on product_specs, which raises PGRST116 on a cache MISS — the normal case — so every miss costs a raised-and-caught exception logged at debug ('L2 specs miss'); same shape at :218 for product_reviews. (d) ADMIN N+1: admin_routes.py:362-380 selects up to N users unbounded, then issues one user_events query PER USER inside a Python for-loop — N+1 against a table with no index (see LS-DB-QUERIES-07). (e) FINGERPRINT FAN-IN: referral_service.py:800 `.select("lifetime_invites_consumed").eq("device_fingerprint_hash", fp)` is unbounded; it is covered by idx_users_device_fp but returns every row sharing a fingerprint with no limit, feeding an abuse cap.
findings.repro: All static reads at HEAD except the row counts and the ~95 KB figure, which come from the live SELECTs in meas_probe.py / meas2.py. (c) confirmed by reading the .single() + `except ... logger.debug(f"L2 specs miss")` pairing at product_data_service.py:76-90.
findings.impact: None of these is harmful at current scale — hence P3 as a group. Ranked by when they start to matter: (a) is the one with no natural ceiling and no owner, and it silently raises the cost of every unbounded scan already reported in this lane; (d) becomes a real admin timeout once the user table grows, and compounds with the missing user_events index; (b) is ~95 KB and two on-loop blocking calls per home screen open; (c) is a hot-path exception on the normal cache-miss branch, which is both slower than a None return and noisy in any profiler; (e) is a correctness risk only if a fingerprint is ever shared widely, in which case the abuse cap reads a truncated set.
findings.fix: (a) Add a retention policy per table in one migration + a scheduled job: search_logs and user_events keep 90 days, admin_audit_log keeps 1 year (check any compliance requirement first), product_prices keep newest N per (product_key, region) as in LS-DB-QUERIES-06. Make the job report to the same place #80 wants cron failures to go. (b) Project the four fields _select_smart_pick actually reads instead of full_response, and wrap both queries in run_db to match the savings path in the same module. (c) Replace `.single()` with `.maybe_single()` (or `.limit(1)` and check the list) so a miss is a None, not a raise. (d) Replace the per-user loop with one `user_events` query using `.in_("user_id", uids)` and group in Python. (e) Add `.limit(50)` and treat hitting the limit as itself an abuse signal. Ship (c) and (e) immediately (both are one-liners with no behaviour change on the success path); (a) needs a product decision on retention windows before it can land.
findings.test_first: For (c), a unit test asserting get_cached_specs returns None for an unknown product_key WITHOUT any exception being raised or logged — red today. For (a), a static test asserting every table in the migration set is named in a retention config file, so a new growth table cannot ship without an explicit keep-forever decision. For (d), a call-counter test asserting the cohort-retention route issues O(1) user_events queries rather than O(users).
findings.dedupe: new — (a) is adjacent to open #80 (cron failure visibility) but that issue presumes crons exist; none of (b)-(e) appear in M18, M13, the mobile checkup or the 33 open issues.

findings.title: Bright Data is the only live search provider today and its spend is unbounded, unmetered and invisible: ENABLE_BRIGHTDATA_BUDGET_GATE is not set in prod
findings.evidence: repro.py through the REAL modules with the exact web knob set: `_brightdata_enabled()=True`, `budget gate enabled=False`, `_bd_budget_precheck()=True (dispatch always allowed)`, `_bd_record is a no-op=True`. `_bd_budget_precheck` (:75) returns True unconditionally when the gate flag is absent; `_bd_record` (:87) returns before `record_usage("brightdata")`. baseline/railway-web-vars.txt lists ENABLE_BRIGHTDATA_FALLBACK=true + BRIGHTDATA_API_KEY + BRIGHTDATA_ZONE=serp_api1 on BOTH web and price-warmer, and does NOT list ENABLE_BRIGHTDATA_BUDGET_GATE on either.
findings.repro: python scratchpad/repro.py (offline; sets only the 12 non-secret knobs baseline/railway-web-vars.txt shows for `web`, pops the knobs absent from that list, imports app.services.brightdata_service + api_budget_service and prints the gate results). Also: `railway variables --service web --kv | grep BRIGHTDATA` shows FALLBACK/KEY/ZONE and no BUDGET_GATE.
findings.impact: Bright Data SERP is the fallback that fires whenever Serper is unavailable — and Serper is at balance -50, so it 403s on every call. Every search leg of every compare therefore dispatches a BILLED Bright Data request with (a) no budget ceiling, (b) no circuit breaker, (c) no per-request meter, and (d) nothing written to the `budget:brightdata:<YYYY-MM>` key, so `/api/v1/admin/costs` reports `brightdata: {used: 0, limit: 4500, remaining: 4500}` forever. Modelled ~12-18 Bright Data requests per cold compare (4-way discovery x2 products + price-organic x2 + unified search x2 + specs/reviews legs; consistent with the ~10-per-cold-lookup measured 2026-08-31), i.e. the packaged 4,500/month free allowance is spent by roughly 250-375 compares and every request after that is billed with no ceiling and no way for the operator to notice.
findings.fix: Set ENABLE_BRIGHTDATA_BUDGET_GATE=true on `web` and `price-warmer`. That single env flip activates the already-written path: `_bd_budget_precheck()` starts consulting `is_circuit_closed("brightdata") and has_budget("brightdata")` against the packaged 4,500/mo ceiling, and `_bd_record()` starts calling `record_usage`/`record_success`/`record_failure`, which is also what makes the provider appear truthfully on /admin/costs. Because the gate fails OPEN on a Redis fault (brightdata_service.py:80-81) the flip cannot manufacture an outage. Do it BEFORE any traffic, and prefer a ceiling declared in an env var rather than the packaged literal so the free-tier number cannot silently darken a paid zone the way SERPER_LIFETIME_LIMIT's 2200 was documented to.
findings.test_first: A test that constructs the exact prod env dict (ENABLE_BRIGHTDATA_FALLBACK=true + key + zone, ENABLE_BRIGHTDATA_BUDGET_GATE unset), monkeypatches `api_budget_service.record_usage`, awaits `brightdata_service.bd_search_web('x')` with `_bd_post` stubbed, and asserts `record_usage` was called at least once. It fails today (0 calls) and passes once the gate is armed. Pair it with a config test asserting that whenever `_brightdata_enabled()` is True, `_brightdata_budget_gate_enabled()` is also True.
findings.dedupe: new

findings.title: The app's main compare shape (product_a/product_b) skips the OpenAI parse and spends a full provider fan-out on a comparison that cannot succeed while OpenAI is dead
findings.evidence: scs@76ace90:3250 `elif explicit_pair:` builds `products` from the two strings with a deterministic `classify_category_from_text` and NEVER calls `parse_product_query` (the OpenAI call is only in the `else:` at :3269). Execution then falls straight into the Phase-1 gather at :3327 `product_data = await asyncio.gather(self._fetch_product_data(products[0]...), self._fetch_product_data(products[1]...))`, which runs the price race, the 4-way Serper/Bright-Data discovery and the render fan-out. SmartCompareApp/src/screens/HomeScreen.tsx:316 sends `{ product_a: productA, product_b: productB }`; text_routes@76ace90:483 rebuilds `q = f"{product_a} vs {product_b}"` so the logged query is indistinguishable. MEASURED in Supabase search_logs: row abec68f8 2026-09-02T01:05:41Z, query 'iPhone 15 vs Galaxy S24', success=false, error='Comparison data was incomplete', duration_ms=31008, cost=0.0 — 31s is the 30s STREAM_HARD_CAP plus overhead, and scs:3112 only returns INSUFFICIENT_DATA when `self._partial_product_data` is already populated, i.e. the fan-out HAD run.
findings.repro: Static + measured. (a) Read scs@76ace90:3250-3330 — no OpenAI call between the explicit-pair branch and the Phase-1 gather, and no OpenAI health/breaker check anywhere on that path. (b) SELECT * FROM search_logs WHERE created_at >= '2026-09-01' — 3 rows, one of which burned the full 31s cap. No live compare is possible (OpenAI 429 insufficient_quota) so this cannot be re-run end-to-end today.
findings.impact: Every compare started from the app's two-field home screen spends real money — the Bright Data SERP requests of finding 01, plus any Firecrawl/Scrape.do render credits the escalation fires — and then fails at specs/verdict because OpenAI is dead. It also holds the single uvicorn worker for the full 30s hard cap, so at the M18 deployment-wide ceiling of ~10 compares/min the whole service is consumed producing nothing. The measured 2026-09-02 sample is 1 of 3 attempts (33%) doing this. Nothing anywhere short-circuits: `'openai' in PROVIDER_CONFIGS` is False (repro.py), so there is no breaker to consult and no signal that the LLM is unavailable before the money is spent.
findings.fix: Add an `openai` entry to `api_budget_service.PROVIDER_CONFIGS` and record success/failure around the 4 AsyncOpenAI clients, then gate the top of `_compare_from_text_impl` on `is_circuit_closed('openai')` behind a new default-OFF flag (e.g. ENABLE_LLM_PREFLIGHT_BREAKER) so flag-OFF is byte-identical. With the breaker open the route should return the existing CONTENT_UNAVAILABLE/503 body BEFORE `_fetch_product_data` and BEFORE any credit is consumed. Cheapest interim mitigation with zero code: while OpenAI has no quota, set ENABLE_BRIGHTDATA_FALLBACK=false on `web` — Serper already 403s, so the search legs degrade to their benign empty shape and the compare fails in ~2s at zero cost instead of 31s at full cost.
findings.test_first: An async test that patches `extraction_service` so every OpenAI call raises a 429, patches `serper_service.search_web`/`search_product_prices` with counting stubs, and calls `service.compare_from_text(query='a vs b', explicit_pair=('a','b'))`. Assert the search stubs were called ZERO times. It fails today (they are called on every leg) and passes once the LLM preflight gate lands.
findings.dedupe: new

findings.title: OpenAI has no budget entry and no circuit breaker anywhere, so a dead key costs up to 6 upstream attempts per verdict and ~23s of the single worker on the cheapest failure path
findings.evidence: repro.py: `PROVIDER_CONFIGS keys = ['brightdata','firecrawl','scrapedo','serper','youtube']`, `openai in PROVIDER_CONFIGS = False`. grep for `is_circuit_closed("openai")` / `record_failure("openai")` in api_budget_service.py returns NO matches. repro.py also measured `openai_max_retries()=2`, `openai_fallback_max_retries()=2`, `verdict_chain_max_attempts()=6` — i.e. prod runs at the shipped default, twice the value model_config.py:204 names as the runbook launch setting ((1+1)+(1+0)=3). url_extraction_service.py:31-35 constructs its AsyncOpenAI with NO max_retries at all. MEASURED: search_logs row b3910305 2026-09-02T01:04:45Z, error='Could not identify two products to compare', duration_ms=22995 — 23 seconds for a request whose only work is one `parse_product_query` call.
findings.repro: python scratchpad/repro.py (prints the PROVIDER_CONFIGS keys and the three retry numbers through the real model_config module) + the search_logs SELECT above. Cannot be exercised live: the key is at 429 insufficient_quota.
findings.impact: Under a 429 storm — or the current permanent-dead-key state — every compare re-attempts the same doomed provider ~10-14 times (parse 1, specs 2, reviews 2, image Tier-3 2, price Tier-3 2, verdict 1 with a 6-attempt chain, plus L3 moderation), each with SDK-level retries and exponential backoff, and nothing ever trips. The measured 22,995 ms for a single failed parse is the concrete cost: the one-worker deployment can serve ~2.6 such requests/minute. At the M18 ceiling of 10 compares/min the loop is 100% consumed by retries against an endpoint that cannot answer, and because `insufficient_quota` never self-heals the state is permanent until a human notices.
findings.fix: Add `"openai": {"monthly_limit": <spend proxy>, "warn_at": ..., "is_lifetime": False}` to PROVIDER_CONFIGS and wrap the 4 client construction sites in a thin helper that calls `record_success`/`record_failure` on the response, then have that helper skip the dispatch when `is_circuit_closed('openai')` is False — all behind a new default-OFF flag so the deploy is byte-identical. Independently and immediately (env only, no deploy): set OPENAI_MAX_RETRIES=1 and OPENAI_FALLBACK_MAX_RETRIES=0 on `web` to move `verdict_chain_max_attempts()` from 6 to 3, which is exactly what #117 built the knobs for and what model_config.py:204 documents as the launch setting. Also give url_extraction_service.py:31 the same `max_retries=openai_max_retries()` the other three clients have.
findings.test_first: A test that patches the AsyncOpenAI client to always raise a 429 and drives `parse_product_query` N times, asserting that after CB_FAILURE_THRESHOLD (3) consecutive failures the (N+1)th call short-circuits without an upstream dispatch. It cannot even be written today because no `openai` provider key exists — that is the finding. Plus a config test: `assert verdict_chain_max_attempts() <= 3` under the prod env dict.
findings.dedupe: known:M18/LS-capacity-math-03 still-open (that finding established the 429 storm triples request volume); the ROOT — that no `openai` entry exists in PROVIDER_CONFIGS so there is no breaker or budget to trip at all, and that prod ships the 6-attempt chain instead of the documented 3 — is new

findings.title: Scrape.do's dead token bills a phantom 5 credits per call and a 401/403 is not a breaker failure, so the dead integration retries forever and silently drains its 900/mo meter
findings.evidence: scs@76ace90:1709-1713 `if cost > 0: record_usage("scrapedo", count=cost)` then `if not html: if status in (429, 503) or status == 0: record_failure("scrapedo")`. 401 and 403 are in NEITHER set, so a dead-token response is METERED but never counted as a failure. scrapedo_service.py:152-159 `_parse_request_cost` returns `int(resp.headers.get("Scrape.do-Request-Cost", 5))` — a 401 with no cost header yields the fallback 5. repro.py measured: `scrapedo is_available()=True` (ENABLE_SCRAPEDO=true + SCRAPEDO_API_TOKEN both present in prod) and `_parse_request_cost(401 resp)=5`. The same shape exists for Firecrawl at scs@76ace90:1630-1634 — `record_usage` only on 200, `record_failure` only on 429/503/0 — so a 402 'out of lifetime credits' is invisible on both axes.
findings.repro: Static (HARD RULE 1 forbids calling Scrape.do). Read scs@76ace90:1674-1721 and scrapedo_service.py:152-198; the status sets are literal. repro.py confirms the flag/token state and the 5-credit fallback through the real `_parse_request_cost`.
findings.impact: The Scrape.do token was documented dead (401) on 2026-06-26 and ENABLE_SCRAPEDO is still true in prod. Every render escalation therefore (a) fires a request that cannot succeed, (b) charges 5 phantom credits to `budget:scrapedo:<YYYY-MM>`, and (c) leaves the breaker CLOSED so the next candidate fires again. After ~180 such 401s the 900-credit meter reads exhausted and `_provider_gate_ok_async('scrapedo')` starts blocking — so the only thing that ever stops the dead integration is a counter of spend that never happened, and it will 'recover' on the 1st of next month and start again. Under burst this is ~2 wasted round trips per render domain per product on the hot 15s price path.
findings.fix: Treat an AUTH/PAYMENT status as a breaker failure and as a no-charge: in `_scrapedo_scraper`, extend the failure set to `status in (401, 402, 403, 429, 503) or status == 0`, and in `_parse_request_cost` return 0 when the header is absent AND the status is >= 400 (a rejected request is not a billed render). Apply the identical widening to `_firecrawl_scraper` at scs:1630-1634. Ship both behind one default-OFF flag (e.g. ENABLE_AUTH_FAILURE_BREAKER) so flag-OFF is byte-identical. Independently, and immediately: set ENABLE_SCRAPEDO=false on `web` and `price-warmer` until a live token exists.
findings.test_first: `test_scrapedo_401_trips_breaker_and_bills_nothing`: stub `render_page_with_status` to return `(None, 401, 5)`, run `_scrapedo_scraper` three times with `record_usage`/`record_failure` spied, and assert `record_usage` was never called and `record_failure` was called 3 times. Today it asserts the exact inverse.
findings.dedupe: new for Scrape.do; the Firecrawl half is known:#61 (Firecrawl cap/half-open/lossy breaker) — still-open, with the fresh detail that a 401/402 is missed by BOTH the meter and the breaker

findings.title: Every in-flight compare at deploy time burns a freemium credit: the refund is a fire-and-forget task created on a loop that is being torn down, and there is no shutdown handler or graceful-shutdown budget
findings.evidence: text_routes@76ace90:685-689 — on the terminal `else` branch of the SSE generator's `finally` (which the comment at :677-684 says runs on CancelledError/GeneratorExit too) the refund is `fire_and_forget(refund_comparison_credit(user_id), label='usage_refund.text_stream.incomplete')`, i.e. `asyncio.create_task` (app/utils/async_utils.py:54). app/main.py has exactly ONE `@app.on_event("startup")` (:168) and ZERO shutdown/lifespan handlers — grep for `on_event(`/`lifespan`/`SIGTERM` across app/ returns only that one line. railway.json's startCommand is `uvicorn app.main:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port $PORT` with no `--timeout-graceful-shutdown`, and Procfile matches. uvicorn is pinned 0.52.4 (requirements.txt:192).
findings.repro: Static; a deploy cannot be triggered under HARD RULE 1. Read text_routes@76ace90:625-699 (the finally's three branches), app/utils/async_utils.py:54, app/main.py:162-172, railway.json.
findings.impact: On SIGTERM uvicorn stops accepting and drains; when the connection finally ends, the generator's `finally` fires and CREATES a brand-new task for the refund (and for `log_search` and `save_comparison_and_track_cohort`). Those tasks have had no chance to run their first Supabase round trip before the loop is closed and pending tasks are cancelled. Result: every compare in flight at deploy time silently burns a free-tier credit (3 lifetime / 10 monthly), loses its history row and loses its analytics row — and because `fire_and_forget` only emits a `logger.warning` (#68), nothing reaches Sentry. Deploys are the routine event here, and each one hits every concurrent user.
findings.fix: Add a shutdown handler that holds a module-level `set()` of live background tasks and awaits them with a bounded `asyncio.wait(timeout=...)`, and pass `--timeout-graceful-shutdown 20` in railway.json's startCommand so uvicorn's drain is bounded and predictable instead of `None` (wait forever). Better still for the credit specifically: make the refund on the terminal branch a direct `await refund_comparison_credit(user_id)` rather than a fire-and-forget — the response is already finished, the extra ~200ms is charged to nobody, and it removes the whole class. Gate the awaited form behind a default-OFF flag (e.g. ENABLE_AWAITED_STREAM_REFUND) so flag-OFF is byte-identical.
findings.test_first: An asyncio test that drives the event_generator to the terminal `else` branch, then immediately closes the loop the way `asyncio.run` does (cancel all pending tasks) and asserts `refund_comparison_credit` never completed. Today it passes (the leak is real); after the fix the awaited refund makes it fail, which is the point — invert the assertion at that commit.
findings.dedupe: new (M18 CD-wave-diffs-02 covers the cold-path-timeout credit burn and CD-interactions-01 the pre-verdict disconnect; neither covers the deploy/SIGTERM path or the missing shutdown handler)

findings.title: All 42 fire-and-forget tasks are created without a strong reference, so CPython may garbage-collect a refund, a history save or an analytics write mid-flight
findings.evidence: app/utils/async_utils.py:54 `task = asyncio.create_task(coro)`; the task is returned but the docstring at :51-52 says 'production callers can ignore the return value', and all 42 production call sites do (text_routes 17, structured_comparison_service 11, auth_routes 5, image_routes 5, feedback_routes 2, auth_service 1, review_service 1 — `grep -rc 'fire_and_forget(' app/`). `add_done_callback` at :66 does not create a strong reference either. runtime.txt pins python-3.12.9, where the event loop tracks tasks in a WeakSet — the exact case the CPython docs warn about ('save a reference to the result of create_task').
findings.repro: Static. Read app/utils/async_utils.py in full (67 lines) and the 42 call sites. Non-deterministic by nature, so it cannot be reproduced on demand — which is precisely why it has never been seen.
findings.impact: A refund (`usage_refund.*`), a history save (`save_comparison.*`), a lifetime counter write or an audit row can vanish with no exception and no log line at all — the done-callback never runs because the task no longer exists. The probability rises with the number of simultaneously-pending tasks, i.e. exactly under the burst this lane is about: 42 sites and several tasks per compare means a 500-app-open burst creates hundreds of concurrently-pending unreferenced tasks. The observable symptom is 'a user's credit was consumed and their comparison is missing from History, and nothing anywhere says why' — indistinguishable from finding 05, which makes both harder to diagnose.
findings.fix: Keep a module-level `_BACKGROUND: set[asyncio.Task] = set()` in async_utils; in `fire_and_forget` do `_BACKGROUND.add(task)` and `task.add_done_callback(_BACKGROUND.discard)` alongside the existing logging callback. Three lines, no flag needed (it can only make tasks MORE likely to complete), and the same set is then the natural thing for the finding-05 shutdown handler to drain. While there, upgrade the `_on_done` warning to a `sentry_sdk.capture_exception(exc)` — that closes #68 in the same edit.
findings.test_first: `test_fire_and_forget_survives_gc`: create a task from a coroutine that awaits an `asyncio.Event`, drop all local references, call `gc.collect()`, then set the event and assert the coroutine ran to completion. Assert `len(async_utils._BACKGROUND) == 1` while pending and 0 after.
findings.dedupe: new

findings.title: DEBUG_STAGE_TIMINGS=true is set on BOTH prod services, adding two blocking Upstash round trips to the event loop per render candidate — against code comments that assert it is a prod no-op
findings.evidence: baseline/railway-web-vars.txt: `DEBUG_STAGE_TIMINGS=true` on `web` AND on `price-warmer`. repro.py measured `firecrawl _diag_enabled()=True` and `scrapedo _diag_enabled()=True` under the prod knob set. scrapedo_service.py:88-97 `_log_invocation` then calls `api_budget_service.get_remaining('scrapedo')` and `get_breaker_state('scrapedo')`; firecrawl_service.py:114-120 is the mirror. Both of those helpers are SYNCHRONOUS `_redis_get` calls (api_budget_service.py `get_remaining` -> `_redis_get(_budget_key(provider))`, `get_breaker_state` -> `_redis_get(_circuit_key(provider))`), and cache_service.py:53-64 `_redis_get` calls `redis_client.get(key)` on an `upstash_redis.Redis` REST client (cache_service.py:28) — a blocking HTTP request. Meanwhile scs@76ace90:5841 states the timing instrumentation is 'gated on DEBUG_STAGE_TIMINGS so it's a true no-op in prod', and scs:7185 repeats 'no-op in prod'.
findings.repro: python scratchpad/repro.py (prints both `_diag_enabled()` results under the exact prod env) + read scrapedo_service.py:85-99, firecrawl_service.py:114-125, api_budget_service.py get_remaining/get_breaker_state, cache_service.py:53-64.
findings.impact: At the M18-measured 163 ms Upstash RTT from Railway, each render candidate pays 2 x 163 ms = ~326 ms of EVENT-LOOP BLOCKING before its request is even sent — and this path is not covered by ENABLE_ASYNC_REDIS_OFFLOAD (neither offload flag is set in prod anyway). A cold compare that fires the render wave on 2 domains x 2 providers x 2 products = 8 invocations pays ~2.6 s of pure diagnostic loop-block, charged to every other concurrent request. It also emits `[PRICE_SUBSTAGE]`/`PRICE_PIPELINE_DIAG` INFO lines on the hot path, inflating log volume per compare. The comments make this invisible to anyone reading the code: they assert the opposite of what prod does.
findings.fix: Set DEBUG_STAGE_TIMINGS=false (or unset it) on `web`; keep it on `price-warmer` only if the off-clock warmer actually needs the attribution. Zero code change, no redeploy for the scs/response_builder readers — though note firecrawl/scrapedo cache the flag in a module global at first read (`_PRICE_PIPELINE_DIAG_FLAG`), so those two need a restart to pick it up. Then fix the two comments (scs:5841 and :7185) to say 'no-op WHEN THE FLAG IS OFF', since 'in prod' is currently false, and move `_log_invocation`'s two Redis reads behind the same offload dispatch the rest of the hot path uses.
findings.test_first: A config test over the captured Railway variable set asserting `DEBUG_STAGE_TIMINGS` is absent or false for the `web` service. Plus a unit test that patches `cache_service._redis_get` with a counter, sets DEBUG_STAGE_TIMINGS=true, calls `scrapedo_service._log_invocation('u')` and asserts the counter is 2 — pinning the cost so the next reader cannot miss it.

findings.title: The only two spend caps present in the Railway config — MAX_MONTHLY_COST and FREE_TIER_DAILY_LIMIT — are read exclusively by functions with zero callers, so setting them does nothing

findings.repro: python scratchpad/repro.py for the resolved values; `rg 'check_monthly_budget|track_api_cost|check_rate_limit|add_api_cost' app/` for the zero call sites.
findings.impact: An operator reading the Railway dashboard sees a $100 monthly cost ceiling and a 5/day free-tier limit and will reasonably conclude spend is capped. Neither is enforced anywhere. The real freemium limiter is `usage_service.TIER_LIMITS` (free daily = 3, not 5) and there is no monthly cost ceiling of any kind in the request path — combined with findings 01 and 03, the deployment has literally zero dollar-denominated spend control. findings.fix: Either delete the four dead functions and the two constants they alone read (M13's recommendation), or — better, given findings 01/03 — wire `MAX_MONTHLY_COST` into a real gate: have `api_budget_service` accumulate a per-provider dollar estimate alongside the existing request counters and short-circuit every paid dispatch when the month's estimate crosses it, behind a default-OFF ENABLE_MONTHLY_SPEND_CEILING. Whichever is chosen, do not leave a variable in the Railway UI that reads like a cap and is not one; if the functions are deleted, remove MAX_MONTHLY_COST and FREE_TIER_DAILY_LIMIT from both services' variables in the same change.

findings.title: Cost accounting excludes every non-OpenAI provider AND every failed compare, so the admin dashboard's monthly total is structurally incapable of showing the spend that is actually happening
findings.evidence: admin_routes.py:127-131: `summary['openai'] = {'cost_usd': ..., 'source': 'comparisons.metadata.total_cost'}` and `summary['estimated_monthly_total'] = round(summary['fixed_costs_monthly'] + openai_cost, 2)` where `fixed_costs_monthly = 30.00` — no Serper, Bright Data, Firecrawl or Scrape.do dollars are in that sum. `total_cost` itself is produced only from OpenAI token pricing (openai_service.py:257 `total_cost = input_cost + output_cost`). On the write side, database_service.py:466-497 `log_search(..., cost: float = 0.0, ...)` and text_routes@76ace90:229-237 — the FAILURE-path `log_search` call passes no `cost=` at all, so every failed compare records 0.0 regardless of what it spent. MEASURED confirmation in search_logs: the three 2026-09-02 rows all have cost=0.0, including the one that ran the full 31s fan-out (abec68f8).
findings.repro: Read admin_routes.py:97-132, openai_service.py:250-263, database_service.py:466-510, text_routes@76ace90:226-275; plus the search_logs SELECT (40 rows, all 2026-09 rows cost=0.0). `get_usage_summary()` (api_budget_service) does list brightdata, but its `used` comes from `record_usage`, which finding 01 shows is never called.
findings.impact: There are three cost surfaces and all three are blind to the money currently being spent. `/admin/costs.estimated_monthly_total` will read $30 + a few cents of OpenAI while Bright Data burns its 4,500/month allowance. `get_usage_summary()` reports brightdata used=0 forever. `search_logs.cost` reads 0.0 for every failure — and while OpenAI is dead, EVERY compare is a failure, so the cost column is guaranteed zero no matter how much is spent. There is no artefact anywhere that would let an operator answer 'what did last month cost'.
findings.fix: Accumulate provider spend the same way OpenAI tokens are accumulated: have `_bd_record`, `_scrapedo_scraper` and `_firecrawl_scraper` add an estimated dollar amount to a per-provider Redis counter, expose those counters in `get_usage_summary`, and include them in `estimated_monthly_total` alongside the $30 fixed cost. Separately and cheaply: pass `cost=result.get('metadata', {}).get('total_cost', 0)` on the FAILURE-path `log_search` calls at text_routes:230 and :386 (the service returns `total_cost` on the INSUFFICIENT_DATA/TIMEOUT bodies — scs@76ace90:3118 and :3126 — so the value is already there and is simply being dropped).
findings.test_first: `test_failed_compare_logs_its_cost`: patch `compare_from_text` to return `{'success': False, 'code': 'INSUFFICIENT_DATA', 'total_cost': 0.004}`, POST /text/compare, and assert the `log_search` spy received `cost=0.004`. It receives 0.0 today. Plus `test_admin_costs_includes_every_paid_provider`: assert `set(summary) >= {'openai','serper','brightdata','firecrawl','scrapedo'}` with dollar values, not just credit counts.
findings.dedupe: adjacent to known:#66 (admin cost meters wrong) — still-open; the two NEW parts are (a) `estimated_monthly_total` is arithmetically OpenAI-only by construction and (b) the failure-path `log_search` drops a `total_cost` the service already returned

findings.title: bd_search_shopping has zero call sites: the Google-Shopping price leg has no Bright Data fallback, so under a Serper 403 it is dead while still paying for a wasted Serper round trip
findings.evidence: `rg 'bd_search_shopping' app/` returns only its definition (brightdata_service.py:238) and no caller — every one of the 8 Bright Data call sites in serper_service.py (:634, :644, :668, :962, :969, :1004, :1016 and the two imports at :629/:958) calls `bd_search_web`. `search_product_prices` (serper_service.py:829-945) — the ONLY shopping entry point — guards on `_active_serper_key()` (:847) and `_serper_budget_ok()` (:854) and then goes straight to `_do_serper_shopping`, with no `_brightdata_enabled()` branch anywhere in the function. Same for `search_product_specs` (:1020), `search_product_reviews` (:1046), `search_videos` (:1068), `search_images` (:1100), `search_news` (:1145), `search_gcc_retailer_prices` (:1224) — 8 of the 10 public entry points have no fallback.
findings.repro: Static; `rg 'bd_search_shopping' app/` and read serper_service.py:829-945. repro2.py demonstrates the contrasting behaviour on `search_web`: 1 wasted Serper POST followed by 1 billed Bright Data POST.
findings.impact: With the Serper key at -50, the shopping tier returns its benign empty shape on every compare — but only AFTER dispatching a live Serper POST that 403s (there is no breaker; see finding 11). So the leg that Google actually has data for is dark, while `search_web`'s legs still spend Bright Data money. The result is a compare that costs full price and loses the price source most likely to succeed, degrading straight to Tier-3 GPT estimates — which then also fail because OpenAI is dead. The dead `bd_search_shopping` is written, tested-shaped and one line from being wired; the ACTIVATION comment at brightdata_service.py:21-23 implies the whole module is live, which is only two-thirds true.
findings.fix: Wire `bd_search_shopping` into `search_product_prices` with exactly the three-branch pattern `search_web` already uses: no-key -> fallback, budget-out -> fallback, exception/non-200 -> fallback, each returning `{**(await bd_search_shopping(product, country)), 'query': product, 'shopping_region': ...}`. Do it behind ENABLE_BRIGHTDATA_BUDGET_GATE being ON first (finding 01), so the new leg is metered from its first call rather than adding a second unbounded spender. Decide explicitly whether the remaining 6 entry points (specs/reviews/videos/images/news/gcc) should fall back or stay dark, and write that decision into the module docstring — right now the asymmetry is undocumented.
findings.test_first: `test_shopping_falls_back_to_brightdata_on_403`: patch `_serper_post` to return a 403 and `bd_search_shopping` with a counting stub, await `search_product_prices('x', 'bh')`, assert the stub was called once and the returned `shopping` list is non-empty. It is called zero times today.
findings.dedupe: new

findings.title: The Serper circuit breaker is written but was never switched on, so every compare fires ~14-18 live POSTs at a key that is guaranteed to 403, each on a fresh TLS connection
findings.evidence: repro.py measured `_serper_breaker_enabled()=False` and `_serper_budget_ok()=True` under the exact prod knob set — ENABLE_SERPER_BREAKER is absent from baseline/railway-web-vars.txt for both services, and SERPER_LIFETIME_LIMIT=0 makes `_serper_gate_engaged()` False (api_budget_service.py:196-197), so the budget gate admits every call too. serper_service.py:330-341 `_serper_record_failure` returns immediately when the flag is off, so the 403-recording branch at :449-450 is inert. The module's own block comment at :286-289 describes exactly this state: 'On the documented 403 state every compare still dispatched all six Serper entry points at their full timeout, per product, forever — no cooldown ever engaged.' repro2.py MEASURED the per-leg shape end-to-end through the real `search_web`: `live Serper POSTs made (wasted) = 1 ['/search']` followed by `live Bright Data POSTs made (BILLED) = 1`.
findings.repro: python scratchpad/repro2.py — patches `serper_service._serper_post` to return a 403 response and `brightdata_service._bd_post` to record, then awaits the REAL `serper_service.search_web('iPhone 15 price bahrain', 10, 'bh')`. Output: 1 wasted Serper POST, 1 billed Bright Data POST, 0 `record_usage` calls.
findings.impact: Modelled per cold compare: ~7-9 Serper entry-point dispatches per product (1 shopping gl=us, 1 price-organic, 4 discovery, 1 unified, 1 images) x 2 products = ~14-18 live HTTPS POSTs to google.serper.dev that are known in advance to 403. Each is issued from a freshly-constructed `httpx.AsyncClient` (no pooling — #73/#70), so each pays a full DNS+TCP+TLS handshake on the single event loop before the 403 lands. That is pure latency and loop occupancy added to a compare that then also pays for Bright Data. Flipping the breaker would collapse all of them to one probe per 10-minute cooldown window.
findings.fix: Set ENABLE_SERPER_BREAKER=true on `web` and `price-warmer`. The path is already written and memoised so it adds no per-call Redis round trip (serper_service.py:311-327), and it fails OPEN on a Redis fault, so the flip cannot manufacture an outage. After 3 consecutive 403s the breaker trips for CB_RECOVERY_TIMEOUT (600s) and the Bright Data fallback is reached directly. Note the ordering constraint: this makes the Bright Data path hotter, so arm ENABLE_BRIGHTDATA_BUDGET_GATE (finding 01) FIRST.
findings.test_first: `test_serper_breaker_trips_on_403_storm`: with ENABLE_SERPER_BREAKER=true, drive `search_web` 5 times against a stubbed 403 and assert the underlying `client.post` was invoked at most CB_FAILURE_THRESHOLD (3) times, not 5. With the flag in its prod state (off) the same test asserts 5 — pin BOTH so the config drift is visible.
findings.dedupe: known:M13-32 (the breaker was built and shipped default-OFF) — status still-dark in prod at 76ace90, with fresh runtime evidence (repro2.py) of the per-leg waste and the ordering constraint against finding 01

findings.title: A shared-bucket 429 reaches the user as a generic 'comparison failed' with no wait-and-retry cue and no Retry-After header, so the burst that caused it gets amplified by immediate retries
findings.evidence: error_handler.py:122-127 `rate_limit_handler` returns `_build_error_response(429, 'Rate limit exceeded. Please try again later.', request_id)` — `_build_error_response` (:41-52) emits `{success, error, code: 'RATE_LIMITED', request_id}` and sets NO `Retry-After` header. Client side at 76ace90: api.ts:146-153 only special-cases `code === 'USAGE_LIMIT'` and otherwise rejects; parseApiError returns `{message: 'Rate limit exceeded...', code: 'RATE_LIMITED'}`; HomeScreen.tsx:394-399 then renders `parsed.code ? t('home.errors.comparison') : ...` — a structured-but-unrecognised code falls to the generic comparison-failed copy. On the SHIPPED bundle (97b5f15) the same block was `Alert.alert(t('common.error'), error.message || ...)`, i.e. the raw axios string 'Request failed with status code 429'. `rg 'RATE_LIMITED|rateLimit' SmartCompareApp/src` finds exactly one handler, in ContactUsScreen.tsx:75, and none on any compare screen.
findings.repro: Static, at both SHAs. Read error_handler.py:36-52 and :122-127; SmartCompareApp/src/services/api.ts:140-180 + parseApiError; HomeScreen.tsx:359-400; `git diff 97b5f15..76ace90 -- SmartCompareApp/src/screens/HomeScreen.tsx` for what phones actually run.
findings.impact: M18 established that every decorated 10/minute limit is ONE deployment-wide bucket keyed on the shared Railway edge IP. So the 11th compare in any minute — from any user anywhere — 429s. That user is told 'we couldn't compare these' (main) or 'Request failed with status code 429' (shipped bundle). Neither says 'wait a minute'; neither is localized as a rate-limit in Arabic; and with no `Retry-After` the client has nothing to back off on. The predictable behaviour is an immediate re-tap, which lands in the same bucket, which extends the outage — a burst of 50 app-opens turns into a self-sustaining 429 storm from a 10/min bucket. This is the user-visible face of the capacity ceiling, and it is the part that makes the ceiling worse instead of degrading gracefully.
findings.fix: Two halves. Backend: have `rate_limit_handler` set a `Retry-After` header from slowapi's `exc.detail` window and include `retry_after_seconds` in the JSON body — a self-contained change in error_handler.py:122. Client: add a `RATE_LIMITED` branch to HomeScreen/ResultsScreen's `onError` (next to the existing `TIMEOUT` branch) that shows dedicated i18n copy in en.json and ar.json ('Lots of people are comparing right now — try again in a moment') and, ideally, disables the compare button for `retry_after_seconds`. Note the two-lever gap: the client half only reaches users on the next `eas update --branch preview`, so ship the backend half first — it at least stops the client from being blind.
findings.test_first: Backend: `test_rate_limit_response_carries_retry_after` — exceed a decorated limit against the TestClient and assert `response.headers['Retry-After']` exists and the body has `retry_after_seconds`. Client: a jest test on HomeScreen's onError with `{response: {status: 429, data: {code: 'RATE_LIMITED'}}}` asserting `Alert.alert` was called with the rate-limit i18n key, not `home.errors.comparison`.
findings.dedupe: known:M18/LS-ratelimit-01 + LS-capacity-math-01 (the shared deployment-wide bucket) — still-open; NEW is the client-facing consequence: RATE_LIMITED has zero handlers on any compare screen, there is no Retry-After, and the resulting immediate-retry loop amplifies the burst

findings.title: Loop saturation is an unrecoverable failure mode: Railway does not health-check a live deployment and restartPolicy only fires on process exit, so a stalled worker is never restarted and the 'max 3 retries' budget is never even consumed
findings.evidence: railway.json:5-10 — `healthcheckPath: '/health'`, `healthcheckTimeout: 30`, `restartPolicyType: 'ON_FAILURE'`, `restartPolicyMaxRetries: 3`. Railway docs (fetched this session, docs.railway.com/deployments/healthchecks): 'Railway does not monitor the healthcheck endpoint after the deployment has gone live' and 'The healthcheck endpoint is currently not used for continuous monitoring'. docs.railway.com/deployments/restart-policy: the policy 'dictates what action Railway should take if a deployed service STOPS, e.g., exits with a non-zero exit code'. app/main.py:307-313 `/health` is an `async def` returning a literal dict — it needs a loop tick, so a loop blocked in synchronous Upstash/Supabase I/O (both offload flags are absent from the prod variable list) cannot serve it. `railway logs --service web` shows one container start at 2026-09-02T15:54:16Z and no restart since.
findings.repro: Static + docs. Read railway.json and app/main.py:300-318; fetch the two Railway doc pages; `railway logs --service web` for the single uninterrupted container lifetime.
findings.impact: Corrects the operational picture M18 recorded. A saturated event loop does NOT exit, so ON_FAILURE never triggers and the 3-restart budget is irrelevant — the deployment simply stops answering, indefinitely, until a human redeploys. Nothing detects it: /health would degrade (it shares the blocked loop, which is the useful part) but #81 is open and nobody polls it, so the degradation is unobserved. Combined with 1 replica x 1 worker this is a single stall away from a silent total outage with no alarm and no auto-recovery. The 30s `healthcheckTimeout` is also 10x tighter than Railway's 300s default; measured cold start is only ~1.3s today, so it is fine now, but it is a deploy-time cliff nobody has written down.
findings.fix: (1) Stand up an external uptime probe against `/health` (Railway's own docs point at the Uptime Kuma template) — that is #81 and it is the ONLY thing that can detect this class. (2) Make `/health` slightly meaningful: have it report event-loop lag (e.g. `time.monotonic()` delta across an `await asyncio.sleep(0)`) so a saturated-but-alive loop is distinguishable from a healthy one, and let the probe alert on lag rather than on a hard timeout. (3) Raise restartPolicyMaxRetries from 3 toward Railway's default 10, since a crash-loop budget of 3 buys nothing but a permanent outage. (4) Add a second uvicorn worker (M18 LS-event-loop-07) so one stalled loop is not the whole service. None of this needs a code flag; (2) is the only code change and is additive.
findings.test_first: Not a unit test — a runbook probe: with the service live, issue N concurrent `/text/compare` requests and poll `/health`, asserting p95 `/health` latency stays under a threshold. That harness is what does not exist, which is the finding. As a code test: `test_health_reports_loop_lag` asserting the /health body contains a `loop_lag_ms` key.
findings.dedupe: known:M18/LS-railway-metrics-03 (zero-HA, ON_FAILURE max 3) and LS-event-loop-09 (healthcheck shares the blocked loop) — still-open, and CORRECTED: the 'max 3 retries then permanent downtime' framing is optimistic, because a stalled loop never exits so ZERO restarts occur and Railway performs no continuous health check at all. Also known:#81 still-open.

findings.title: P3 sweep: five latent cost/observability nits on the burst path
findings.evidence: (a) model_router_service.py:86-93 `_get_4o_usage_today` is an `async def` that calls the SYNCHRONOUS `_redis_get` with no `asyncio.to_thread` branch — it is covered by NEITHER ENABLE_ASYNC_REDIS_OFFLOAD nor ENABLE_SYNC_DB_OFFLOAD, so it is an unconditional ~163ms loop block on every `priority='high'` model selection. (b) brightdata_service.py:149-158 logs a full `[brightdata] parsed OK ... top-keys=... org0_keys=...` line at INFO on EVERY successful Bright Data call — modelled ~12-18 INFO lines per cold compare from this one site alone, on the provider that is currently serving every search. (c) railway.json:7 sets `healthcheckTimeout: 30` against Railway's 300s default; measured cold start is ~1.3s (`railway logs`: container start 15:54:16.48 -> 'Application startup complete' by 15:54:17.49) so there is headroom today, but the margin is undocumented and a heavier import tree fails the DEPLOY with no other signal. (d) STREAM_HARD_CAP_SECONDS=30 in prod while the code default is 25.0 (scs@76ace90:1365) and every Phase-1 budget comment reasons against 25 (e.g. scs:4631 'KEPT at 15 — raising to 18 would risk the 30s STREAM_HARD_CAP'), so the sizing rationale and the shipped value are documented inconsistently. (e) app/main.py:288 advertises `"docs": "/docs"` from `GET /` while :91-92 disables docs_url whenever RAILWAY_ENVIRONMENT is set — the public root points at a 404 in prod.
findings.repro: Static reads at 76ace90: model_router_service.py:86-93 (and `rg 'ENABLE_ASYNC_REDIS_OFFLOAD' app/services/model_router_service.py` -> no matches); brightdata_service.py:149-158; railway.json; `railway logs --service web` head; repro.py (`STREAM_HARD_CAP_SECONDS (env-resolved) = 30.0`) against scs:1365; app/main.py:275-298.
findings.impact: Individually small; each shows up under burst. (a) adds an uncovered blocking round trip per verdict on the single loop, in the one module whose docstring claims it is 'stateless beyond the Redis-backed daily counter'. (b) makes per-compare log volume scale with the provider fan-out precisely when an operator most needs to read the log. (c)/(d) are documentation-vs-reality drift on two numbers that bound the deploy and the request clock. (e) is cosmetic but is the first thing anyone probing the API sees.
findings.fix: (a) Route `_get_4o_usage_today` through the same `_cache_get_async` dispatch the rest of the hot path uses, so it inherits ENABLE_ASYNC_REDIS_OFFLOAD. (b) Demote the `parsed OK` line to DEBUG, or keep it at INFO only for the first call per process the way `_log_serper_gate_config_once` does. (c) Either raise healthcheckTimeout back toward the 300s default or add a CI assertion that import+startup stays under it. (d) Make 30.0 the code default in scs:1365 so code and prod agree, and update the budget comments that cite 25. (e) Drop the `docs` key from the root payload when RAILWAY_ENVIRONMENT is set, reusing the existing `_openapi_url()` predicate.
findings.test_first: One config test per item is enough: `test_stream_hard_cap_default_matches_prod` (assert scs.STREAM_HARD_CAP_SECONDS default == the Railway value), `test_root_does_not_advertise_disabled_docs` (set RAILWAY_ENVIRONMENT, GET /, assert 'docs' not in endpoints), and a counting test that `model_router.get_model('high')` performs its Redis read through the offload dispatch.
findings.dedupe: new (each item is new; (a) sits adjacent to known:#71 Redis/Supabase off loop — still-open — as a call site neither offload flag covers)
